clue.text: "Some mute Milton here may rest." (Gray)

parts.note: a line from Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard with one adjective dropped out; the solver supplies the missing word describing the unknown, uncelebrated Milton

explanation.surface: A quotation from Gray's Elegy about an obscure poet buried in a country churchyard.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed page shows a dash where the word belongs: the full line reads 'Some mute ... Milton here may rest', the gap being the answer. Gray's Elegy is a famous eighteenth-century English poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray imagines a villager with Milton's gifts who died unknown and without fame, the word in the gap meaning lacking glory or renown.

clue.text: European in charge no way to come first!

indicators.note: says the words before it are placed ahead of the abbreviation for in charge

parts.note: taken as written
RD is the abbreviation for road, a way

explanation.surface: An exclamation that someone from Europe in a position of authority must never be put first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to come first' moves NO RD ahead of IC, although the clue prints IC first.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scandinavian or other northern European person is described by this word, so it stands for a kind of European.

clue.text: A period of perpetual spring?

parts.note: spring is read not as the season but as jumping, so a period of constant springing is a jumping year

explanation.surface: A dreamy wish for a time when spring weather never ends.
explanation.walkthrough: Spring looks like the season of blossom; it is the verb, to jump or bound.
explanation.definitionFit: The calendar year with an extra February day carries the name of a jump, so it is jokingly a year of endless springing.

clue.text: Withdrawal bringing Carter into revolution

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the letters of Carter and into are churned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An ex-president being caught up in an uprising leads to someone backing down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' looks like a link telling you where Carter goes, but it is part of the fodder: CARTER plus INTO, rearranged by 'revolution'.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking back a statement or pulling back from a position is a withdrawal, the formal word for such a climbdown.

clue.text: Striking actors a man rejected

parts.note: workers on strike are said to be out
the actors in a play make up its cast

explanation.surface: Performers on strike shun one of their colleagues.
explanation.definitionFit: A pariah is a person thrown out by society, someone rejected and shunned by others.

clue.text: Piles up for a while

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for piles is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: the pile of a carpet or velvet is its nap, so piles are naps

explanation.surface: Something accumulates over a period of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piles up' reads as accumulates; Piles is the fabric surface, NAPS, and 'up' turns it round in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: A span of time is a stretch or period, so the word means a while.

clue.text: A little cash is very much the object!

parts.note: far means by a great deal, as in far better
an object is a thing

explanation.surface: Someone insists that a small sum of money matters most of all.
explanation.walkthrough: The old British farthing was a quarter of a penny, withdrawn in 1961.
explanation.definitionFit: The coin was worth a quarter of an old penny, the smallest amount of British money in its day.

clue.text: Where food is cooked by turns

definitions.text: Where food is cooked by turns

parts.words: Where food is cooked by turns
parts.note: by turns suggests taking it in turns, but here the meat is cooked by being turned round on a spit

explanation.surface: A kitchen where cooks take turns at the stove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by turns' looks like 'alternately'; it really means by rotating.
explanation.definitionFit: A spit-roasting device, or the restaurant using one, cooks meat as it revolves in front of heat.

clue.text: King Edward is to shoot at duck

parts.note: to pot is to shoot game, as in a pot shot
taken as written
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, O

explanation.surface: A king is planning to fire his gun at a waterfowl.
explanation.walkthrough: King Edward is a popular British variety of potato, not a monarch. A duck is a zero score in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: King Edward is a well-known variety of the tuber, so it is an example standing for the vegetable.

clue.text: Flier puts it on a moving target

indicators.note: it is attached on the end, after the rearranged target
target is set moving, its letters shifted into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A marksman's prey is a bird darting about across the range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' rearranges TARGET to GREATT, and 'on' puts IT after that.
explanation.definitionFit: This common garden songbird flies, so it is a kind of flier.

clue.text: This may well get thrown at the match

definitions.text: This may well get thrown at the match

parts.words: This may well get thrown at the match
parts.note: match suggests a sporting fixture where missiles get thrown, but it is a marriage, where paper scraps are showered on the couple

explanation.surface: Something hurled at a football game by unruly fans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'match' means a marriage, not a game.
explanation.definitionFit: Guests shower newlyweds with little bits of coloured paper as they leave a wedding.

clue.text: A measure taken more than once by the Crusaders

definitions.text: taken more than once by the Crusaders

explanation.surface: A unit of land repeatedly seized by medieval knights.
explanation.walkthrough: Acre is also a port in present-day Israel, captured and recaptured during the Crusades.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: a unit of land area of 4,840 square yards, and a coastal city in the Holy Land that changed hands several times in the Crusades.

clue.text: A majestic disclaimer

parts.note: majestic hints at grandeur, but means belonging to a monarch, and the disclaimer is a renunciation of the throne

explanation.surface: A grand, lofty denial of responsibility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'majestic' is read as 'of a Majesty': a king or queen giving up the crown, as Edward VIII did in 1936.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch formally renouncing the crown is giving up a claim, a royal act of relinquishment.

clue.text: Irregular liaisons can result in people being hurt

parts.note: casual work or visits are irregular, occasional
liaisons are links or connections, ties

explanation.surface: A warning that occasional love affairs can end in heartbreak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irregular liaisons' looks like anagram fodder plus indicator, but the letters do not fit; each word is a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Victims injured or killed in an accident or battle are the wounded and dead, those who got hurt.

clue.text: The singer to obsess a girl completely

parts.note: an alto is a singer with a low female or high male voice
to get to someone is to preoccupy or irritate them
her refers to any female, a girl

explanation.surface: A vocalist becomes fixated on a young woman entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means wholly or in total, as in 'not altogether happy'.

clue.text: The city tried to change

indicators.note: the letters of tried and to are altered into a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A city attempted to reform itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' reads as part of 'tried to change' but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Detroit in Michigan is a major American city, famous for car making.

clue.text: Having the timing right, almost everybody will be civil

parts.note: tempo is the pace or timing of a piece of music

indicators.note: almost means the word for everybody is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: all means everybody

explanation.surface: With good timing, nearly everyone will behave politely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'civil' looks like 'polite' but means secular, non-church, which is the answer's sense of worldly as against spiritual.
explanation.definitionFit: Lords temporal sit in Parliament by secular right, unlike bishops, so the word means civil rather than ecclesiastical.

clue.text: Celebrity harbours recurrent urge to shock

indicators.note: harbours means holds within, so the word for celebrity encloses the other piece

parts.note: a celebrity is a star

indicators.note: recurrent is read as running back, so the word for urge is turned round

parts.note: to egg on is to urge

explanation.surface: A famous person keeps a repeated impulse to scandalise people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recurrent' reverses EGG to GGE, which 'harbours' places inside STAR.
explanation.definitionFit: To astonish or astound someone is to stagger them, leaving them reeling.

clue.text: Making a bloomer, may turn red again!

indicators.note: the letters of red again are turned about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who has made a blunder blushes once more.
explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer is British slang for a blunder, but here it is literally something that blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: The fragrant white-flowered shrub produces blooms, so it is jokingly a bloomer.

clue.text: He'll get the cleaner in free

indicators.note: the cleaner is put in, inside the word for free

parts.note: to rid is to free
a char, or charwoman, is a British word for a cleaning lady

explanation.surface: A man will have his cleaner come in for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He'll' defines a man's name, as many crosswords do with 'he'. CHAR is a British cleaning lady.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard is a male first name, so a man who will do something can be him.

clue.text: To make some improvement in appearance is encouraging

indicators.note: the improving word goes in, inside the word for appearance

parts.note: a coming is an arrival or appearance
to mend is to repair or improve

explanation.surface: Smartening oneself up a bit is a cheering sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in appearance' reads as 'in looks'; really MEND goes inside COMING.
explanation.definitionFit: Praising someone is giving them heart, so commending is encouraging.

clue.text: To do with imbibing at speed

indicators.note: imbibing means taking in, so the word for about swallows the other piece

parts.note: re means about, to do with
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something about drinking quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: A rate is a pace, as in at a great rate, so it means speed.

clue.text: The lessee is "X", a social worker

parts.note: X is the Roman numeral ten
ants are social insects, and worker ants do the colony's labour

explanation.surface: Someone renting a property is a former social worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'social worker' is not a welfare officer: ants live in colonies and workers forage.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who leases a property from a landlord is its occupant who pays rent.

clue.text: Comprehensive, even if unfinished

parts.note: tho is the informal short spelling of though, even if
rough means unfinished, as in a rough draft

explanation.surface: A complete job, even though not quite done.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorough investigation covers every detail, so it is complete and comprehensive.

clue.text: One consumes a little because required to do so

indicators.note: a little of the words because required is taken, a short run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: A person takes only a small amount because they are told to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a little' signals a short run within 'because required'. 'to do so' is linking surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A user is someone who consumes something, such as a drug or a product.

clue.text: Greek article followed by one other article

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
then means next, followed by
I is the Roman numeral one
an is the other form of the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A grammar note about a Greek definite article followed by another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'followed by' looks like a charade signal but supplies THEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Athens, the Greek capital, is a Greek.

clue.text: Coloured circle on compass

parts.note: the letter O is round like a circle
compass means scope or range

explanation.surface: A coloured ring marked on a navigational instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'compass' is scope, not the direction finder.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes something of the colour between red and yellow, so it means coloured that hue.

clue.text: Crumbled bread lies around for the birds

indicators.note: the word for lies goes around the rearranged bread

parts.note: lies means rests, reclines

indicators.note: crumbled bread is broken up, so its letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Broken bread scattered about as food for garden birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crumbled' turns BREAD into DBREA, which RESTS goes 'around'.
explanation.definitionFit: Robins are often called by this name for their red chests, so they are birds.
